rv.q: It also hints at the beguiling, dreamlike circularity of Thomas’s writing. There’s superb acting from a multitasking cast. Siân Phillips is a demure Polly Garter, while Alan David and Cleo Sylvestre spit venom as the Pughs, a couple trapped in a comically poisonous marriage.
Sheen gropes for words, and new-mints his verbal prods; Thomas's text sounds far from emptily declamatory, and its fragmented style acquires a new kind of inner logic.
His performance is magnetic and charged with emotion, the moment of breakthrough between father and son immensely moving.

In Lyndsey Turner’s Olivier staging of Under Milk Wood, his galvanising presence and knack for whipping up a storm with words make a strong and emotionally satisfying case for this popular verse drama by Dylan Thomas.
Lyndsey Turner's richly cast production at the National changes that.
Nor could you wish for a more loquacious, richer narrator than hirsute, woody-voiced Sheen, who looks like he's been training outside an off-licence.
Less a work of drama than a linguistic ritual, the half-whimsical, half-eldritch murmurings of Dylan Thomas’s masterwork ‘Under Milk Wood’ don’t really allow for broad interpretation.
Director Lyndsey Turner fully milks the satirical but tender poignancy of the writing with the aid of a strong, mostly Welsh cast.
Turner's production hovers in an uneasy place between reading and performance, muddying some of the music and beauty of the text.
Still, the evening seems, to me, misconceived.
To hear Michael Sheen deliver Under Milk Wood feels akin to witnessing Gielgud's Hamlet or Rylance's Rooster Byron. It is nothing short of theatrically seminal.

There's commanding, and then there's Michael Sheen, who sweeps on to the Olivier stage 15 minutes or so into the new National Theatre revival of Under Milk Wood and scoops up the entire production with it. Inheriting a role made to order for this Welshman, Sheen takes to his fellow countryman Dylan Thomas's 1954 classic as if on a date with destiny.
It is a bravura performance, lacking the intimacy of radio, but reaching out to the audience.
Under Milk Wood delivers on stage as well.

Why do we tell stories? Lyndsey Turner’s emotive staging of Dylan Thomas’s 1953 play for voices proffers some profound ideas: to heal familial bonds, to find lucidity in the murkiness of dementia, and to reach much-needed catharsis after a long period of suffering.
This is a decent and enjoyable show despite the NT's attempts to punish the audience for turning up.
But for all the attempts at contextualizing for added emotional weight, the effort shows.

And I hadn’t read or heard Under Milk Wood , Dylan Thomas’ play-for-voices, for decades. Actually, not since those cheesy-listening tracks were the grownups’ hip-hop. I remember being thrilled aged eight to find out, against parental intention, that the village of Llareggub whose day the poet relates is a palindrome of “bugger all”.
It's thrilling to see a veteran cast light up the stage and Sheen's passionate narration allows Thomas' poetic prose to soar once more.
